title: Faisal Islam: What I learned from a week with the world's top finance leaders
description: When it comes to the future direction of the global economy there is a bit of a tug of war going on.There are starkly opposing forces. On the one hand
body: When it comes to the future direction of the global economy there is a bit of a tug of war going on.There are starkly opposing forces. On the one hand holding back growth are the familiar, recurring crises from the energy shock, trade conflict and actual war. This is reflected most clearly in the sharply rising interest rate costs for the world's advanced economies. Pulling in the other direction is the boost from massive spending on AI, and the frankly astonishing resilience shown especially by smaller economies, as new routes for trade, including for oil and gas, have been established out of necessity.At the IMF meetings in Bangkok this week these themes came up again and again, including among those at the very top table. But not even they know which way things are going to go.In the meantime it's a sportsman's bet where the roving eye of the bond markets will focus next. Currently they seem to be looking at the US and France.However, the French finance minister, Roland Lescure, has been telling the world he has had no problem selling debt, though it was more expensive, and that his Budget would be fine. He also suggested he had helped save the G7 group of advanced nations, which was at risk of collapsing a year ago amid Donald Trump-inspired tensions.In some ways it is a miracle there has not been a global recession, or a debt crisis in a major emerging economy. Indeed the Thai finance minister was boasting to me of how little his borrowing costs had gone up, especially in relation to the US.Another surprise is the UK being taken off the bond markets' naughty step, and instead being named model pupil by the IMF. The IMF has taken the government's Budget plans at face value and on trust. The reality is that the rest of the G7 lack even this. And beauty is relative, especially when it comes to borrowing.And this moment gave Chancellor John Healey the chance of a hearing, to highlight that the UK's actual growth data has continued to outperform expectations and so far in 2026 can now be described as strong. Healey told me that he saw the figures as the first sign that AI and tech investment was starting to increase UK economic growth. The bond financiers milling around the IMF meetings seem to be taking another look at the UK after years of crisis.But there is a third big challenge to wrestle with, on top of geopolitical instability and bond market uncertainty, one that's apparent even on the streets of Bangkok, as the chauffeurs dropped off the bankers and finance ministers for this week's gathering.Like other nations Thailand has experienced first hand the astonishing boom in sales of Chinese electric vehicles. Thailand is sometimes dubbed the "Detroit of Asia" for its own strong car making heritage. Now nearly a third of all car sales are  Chinese EVs.It is the clearest example of what is known as the China Shock Two. The sheer speed of China's dominance in advanced manufacturing. The first China shock came in the 2000s in basic manufacturing.This second wave of dramatic change has led in just the last few months to a reappraisal of how world trade is functioning and how it is going to be managed. This is especially the case in the EU, which is scrambling to reassess what currently feels like a one-way street when it comes to China-Europe trade.The extra "Made in Europe" protections that the bloc is drawing up will have a profound impact on the UK too. If the UK is outside the new rules, China could divert its excess car production to the UK, where, like Thailand, there are currently lower tariffs and even subsidies. Or the EU could invite Britain in, but ask it to follow its suit by raising tariffs to match its own.Then there is the sub-plot of the UK's relationship with the European Union. This was a theme that cut through more than might have been expected in Bangkok this week and even seemed to provide a little entertainment. The managing director of the IMF Kristalina Georgieva rolled with laughter, suggesting the Brexit "divorcees are now dating again". The Finnish finance minister told me the UK was "flirting" with the EU. Major banks were issuing reports about the prospect of "Breturn".It is, however, the AI boom that is being relied on to provide the trampoline that is required to bounce the world economy out of its current era of multiple simultaneous crises, so many of which are linked to the decisions of President Trump. But even that is not clear cut. In one room the transformative economic effect of AI is lionised by finance ministers. In the next, central bankers fret about its power to break the cybersecurity of most of the banking system. The financial boom around it can't last. The masters of the financial universe are just thankful that it has so far.

schema.headline: Faisal Islam: What I learned from a week with the world's top finance leaders

title: Inside Brooklyn novelty shop at centre of 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
description: On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.Inside,
body: On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby in this Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000)."Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a  shop, who imply she cannot afford various items.In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable".Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale. It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000.They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day."Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said. "It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit.The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird.She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier.But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises. One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy. For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise.Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days. Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here."I really like it here."

schema.headline: Inside Brooklyn novelty shop at centre of 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird

title: Katie Zacharia was thrown into a whirlwind - and failed at a critical time for Trump
description: The White House press secretary job is a challenging one, even under the best of circumstances.These were not the best of circumstances.Katie Zacharia
body: The White House press secretary job is a challenging one, even under the best of circumstances.These were not the best of circumstances.Katie Zacharia was thrown into the whirlwind, joining the White House team as press secretary just weeks away from what polls suggest could be a difficult midterm congressional elections for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.In just five days, she was out – the result of a disastrous press conference that lasted all of 14 minutes, followed by a series of halting media appearances and questions about whether she had mischaracterised her legal credentials over the course of her career.The axe dropped on Friday, with the news delivered – in a roundabout way - by Trump himself before the gathered media at the White House, as he recounted a conversation he had with Zacharia earlier in the day."Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider," Trump said he told Zacharia. "Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this."He later added that maybe the press secretary job "is not for her".In case there was any doubt, the White House quickly confirmed to the BBC that Zacharia would be "transitioning" out of her current job.Trump may be wondering whether Zacharia "needs" the press secretary job, but presidents – including this one - benefit most from a competent press secretary in times of crisis.And while there may not be an immediate crisis, this White House is certainly facing growing adversity.Across the US, Republican candidates are scrambling to hold on to their seats in the upcoming elections. Some are doing so by distancing themselves from the president and his policies, creating new stresses and faultlines within a party that has for so long been broadly unified behind Trump.Meanwhile, the White House has been beset by a series of controversies – including allegations of corruption that forced the resignation of US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and an abrupt reversal of plans to publicly air a military execution in December after widespread bipartisan backlash.A skilled press secretary may have been able to navigate these political landmines while continuing to push out the White House's preferred message in the face of a building media frenzy.Karoline Leavitt, who worked as Trump's press secretary from the start of his second term until she resigned in August a few months after welcoming her second child, proved highly adept at defending the administration from the press room lectern while avoiding stumbles and maintaining a collegial relationship with journalists.Her performance set a high bar for Zacharia, who was a relative novice. It was a mark she failed to reach or even approach, although she never really had much of a chance.The speed at which she failed was astounding, setting a modern record for the shortest-tenured White House press secretary.Zacharia's halting Tuesday press conference performance, combined with those questions about her legal background, essentially sealed her fate.And subsequent press appearances, including a less-than-welcoming interview with conservative pundit Sean Hannity on Thursday – which Trump said he watched – did nothing to change that.As president, Trump has essentially acted as his own press secretary, making major announcements and changing policies from the Oval Office, the White House lawn, airfield tarmacs – wherever he happens to be.Zacharia herself noted this phenomenon prior to being tabbed for the White House job. "President Trump does not need a spokesperson," she posted on X. "He is his own best press secretary."Now, he will have to be.Trump's penchant for speaking off the cuff, however, has made the job a difficult one over the course of his two terms in office.His press secretaries have sometimes had their public statements undermined by presidential pronouncements. At other times, they've been left out of the loop of key decisions.When they have been effective, they have managed to ride the choppier waves while also smoothing relations with the media - providing context for inquisitive journalists and helping tamp down any simmering issues.In comments to Fox News on Friday, Trump said that he is in "no rush" to find a new press secretary. But at such a critical time in his second term, Trump will be without the help that someone like Leavitt offered so consistently.He may come to regret not having it.

schema.headline: Katie Zacharia was thrown into a whirlwind - and failed at a critical time for Trump

title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
description: Donald Trump has blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr
body: Donald Trump has blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens.The sanctions were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by Trump in September. But the US president issued an executive order on Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US "national interest", prompting a backlash from US lawmakers.Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed last week, after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel. Ukraine then accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support. Trump and Zelensky have since exchanged sharp words about one another. Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin.The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy, giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.Many of these provisions have now been waived by Trump.Democrats including the Virginia Congressman Don Beyer have criticised the move, accusing Trump of capitulating to Moscow and turning his back on Kyiv and Zelensky. "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer wrote on X. The move is likely to draw further anger from Ukraine, where Zelensky has long stressed the need for stringent sanctions to limit funding Russia can use in its war effort.Trump was initially criticised by Zelensky and Ukraine's European allies for temporarily suspending some US sanctions to import Russian diesel in a bid to bring down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.Trump has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Middle East conflict, which has sent fuel costs soaring ahead of the US midterm elections. Rising inflation has soured Trump's standing with the American public.Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.A few days later, Trump claimed that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" to facilitate the export of Russian diesel. Both nations have been intensively striking one another's energy infrastructure. Kyiv says this is to limit revenue for Russia's war machine, while Moscow claims it only targets facilities used by the Ukrainian military.Zelensky initially expressed surprise at Trump's announcement, and said Kyiv would stop the strikes if Russia did the same. After three days which saw several fresh attacks from Russia, Kyiv resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries.This prompted scathing condemnation from Trump, who called the strikes a "disgrace". Zelensky replied that he was "only standing up for Ukraine's interests". Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine.  Last week Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield missions, Ukraine said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks. During the slowdown, Russia launched several deadly strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying these came with no prior warning.Zelensky said on Friday that Starlink speeds had still not been fully restored.Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing and deliberately slowing down Ukraine's Starlink network.Additional reporting by Helen Sullivan

schema.headline: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies

title: Brazil sees record fall in Amazon deforestation as key election looms
description: Jair Bolsonaro promoted mining in indigenous lands in the Amazon and forest clearances soared at the same time as resources to protect the forest were
body: Jair Bolsonaro promoted mining in indigenous lands in the Amazon and forest clearances soared at the same time as resources to protect the forest were cut.During Bolsonaro's presidency from 2019 to 2022, the Amazon lost nearly 60% more in forest lands compared to the previous four years, news agency AFP reported, citing official data.Lula reversed his policies and oversaw deforestation rates drop to a six-year low during his first year in office. Lula tightened up environmental monitoring and penalties for illegal logging."Our goal is to achieve zero illegal deforestation by 2030," he said in a post on X on Friday.Tropical rainforests like the Amazon are home to millions of species. In a healthy state, they absorb vast quantities of planet-warming carbon dioxide, helping to keep the Earth cool.But they have come under increasing pressure from decades of deliberate land clearance for agriculture and logging, as well as climate change, which scientists warn can create conditions for wildfires.Brazil's Environment Minister Joao Paulo Capobianco described the decline in Amazon deforestation as "absolutely stratospheric".It was an "historic achievement" for Brazil, said Marcio Astrini, executive secretary at climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima.It showed that "with political will, it is possible to curb deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions", Astrini said.

schema.headline: Brazil sees record fall in Amazon deforestation as key election looms

title: Barack Obama awarded honorary degree from Queens University Belfast
description: Obama receives honorary degree from Queen's University BelfastImage source, Queen's UniversityImage caption, Obama gave an acceptance speech in which
body: Obama receives honorary degree from Queen's University BelfastImage source, Queen's UniversityImage caption, Obama gave an acceptance speech in which he discussed the peace process, the fragility of democracy and the role of young people in shaping Northern Ireland's futureByEmmet McElhattonBBC News NIFormer US President Barack Obama has been awarded an honorary degree from Queen's University Belfast (QUB).Receiving his doctorate, the 44th US president praised Northern Ireland's progress and challenged the next generation to continue building a peaceful and inclusive future.The Good Friday Agreement peace agreement "is still a shining example of what can happen when people put aside old wounds and choose peace," he told university staff and students. During his visit to Northern Ireland, Obama was due to address an audience of paying fans in Belfast's O2 Arena on Tuesday night.Image source, Queen's UniversityImage caption, Obama spoke and shook hands with students during his time in Belfast Accepting the honorary doctorate during a special ceremony at QUB, Obama made a speech that touched on a number of subjects including the peace process and the role young people can play in shaping Northern Ireland's future.Obama said that, while peace had transformed opportunities across Northern Ireland, its benefits must continue to be shared by all.Comparing Northern Ireland now to the place he encountered on a visit back in 2013, he said young people today faced significant challenges but also had reasons to remain hopeful."But," he added, "as we have seen in many countries, including in my home country the United States, peace and democracy are not inevitable. "They have to be chosen, again and again."'Keep showing the way'During the ceremony, Obama heard from Emma McAllister, a first-year Law with Politics student from north Belfast.McAllister first engaged with Queen's through a cross-community programme that helped young people from the Ardoyne and Shankill areas to access leadership and educational opportunities.After listening to McAllister, Obama said: "That's what peace makes possible. And it's what Queen's and the supporters in this room are helping to make real."In his closing remarks, Obama set out a challenge for students."And that is to keep showing the way," he said.Queen's President and Vice-Chancellor Professor Sir Ian Greer congratulated Obama. "We are privileged to welcome President Obama to Queen's. "His commitment to peace, dialogue and public service has left a lasting impact around the world, and particularly here in Northern Ireland."Why does QUB award honorary degrees?According to the university, honorary degrees are awarded to those who have achieved distinction or given significant service in one or more of a number of broad constituencies. This includes business and commerce, the arts, education, medicine, and more.In 2025, former Manchester United footballer Gary Neville received a QUB honorary degree for his contribution to sport, business, education and philanthropy.Other notable recipients include boxer Carl Frampton, poet Seamus Heaney, former Irish President Mary McAleese and playwright Brian Friel.

schema.headline: Barack Obama awarded honorary degree from Queens University Belfast

title: Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC
description: Italy's defence minister has said it was a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used b
body: Italy's defence minister has said it was a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks.Guido Crosetto warned in a BBC interview that any such move by US President Donald Trump's administration "makes absolutely no sense" and risked prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to bring peace.US officials have said Trump has not asked for the slowdown of internet speeds the US provides to Ukraine and which are vital for its war effort. Trump has also denied that the US has stopped sharing early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks with Ukraine. Crosetto's comments continue Italy's sharpening criticism of the US.Earlier this week, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called Trump's deal to buy diesel from Russia a "very risky choice" and said it would "grant Russia legitimacy" as it bombed cities in Ukraine.Trump agreed the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, blaming Kyiv's own attacks on Russian refineries for rising fuel prices.Meloni, once considered so close to the US president she was dubbed a "Trump whisperer", said the move ran counter to efforts to bring Putin to the negotiating table."Peace will come when Putin is convinced there is a stalemate, that he cannot advance any further," her defence minister told the BBC at his ministry building in Rome.Crosetto was a co-founder of Meloni's hard-right Fratelli d'Italia party, which has led a right-wing government coalition since 2022, shortly after the start of Russia's full-scale war."If [Putin] sees weakness on the Ukrainian side – and if the US deprives Ukraine of resources, that creates weakness – then he will believe he can win. So he will continue the war," Crosetto warned."I think that is completely wrong."Despite widespread public scepticism, Meloni's Italian government has been a strong ally of Ukraine from the start, sending both military and humanitarian aid.The specifics of those deliveries have always been classified.Crosetto vowed that Italian military support would continue "for as long as this government is in place", though he warned that getting Italy's parliament to approve further deliveries would be "more difficult" as elections approached.The vote has to take place by the end of 2027 and opinion polls currently put a new far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, ahead of all Meloni's coalition partners.That party's leader, former general Roberto Vannacci, is openly sympathetic to Russia and opposes aiding Ukraine, arguing that Europe is wasting its money as Russia's military "continues to advance" on the ground.At a recent event in Tuscany, he described himself as "neither pro-Putin nor pro-Russian" but "pro-Italian".Crosetto brushed off questions about Vannacci, including on whether his views reflected those of many Italians, saying he had more "serious matters to deal with".But, perhaps to underline the difference, he was unequivocal on Russia."When one state crosses another state's border with tanks, when it bombs hospitals and schools, kills civilians and bombs power plants, and has been doing so for four years, I can only describe that as evil," he said.But Italians, like many Europeans, are seeing prices go up, driven by the high cost of energy.During street protests in Rome on Friday, where firecrackers were thrown, secondary school students complained that resources were being diverted to arms instead of education.Some chanted: "We want more classroom, not more bombs."In southern Italy, truckers have begun blocking roads complaining at the hike in fuel prices.Polls here regularly show that a majority of Italians want an end to military aid for Ukraine. One, conducted for the Ixè institute in September, put support for continuing to supply arms at just 18%.There are many factors behind that, from a long-standing pacifist tradition to a history of strong business ties to Moscow. Unlike Poland or the Baltic states, Italy feels physically distant from the danger, too.But the defence minister also blamed an active campaign of disinformation by Moscow – targeting, he said, "certain political figures... and narratives to weaken the political climate against Russia"."In some way they shift public opinion," the minister argued."It's very hard to explain to a citizen who's having trouble at the petrol pump that we can't give any concessions to Russia right now. But that's the only way to defend the future of that very citizen who's complaining."Italy has not been targeted for major acts of sabotage, unlike other allies of Ukraine in Europe.The minister said a fire at an arms depot outside Rome in August was not arson, but "human stupidity".A report last month that Russia was planning to launch drone attacks at Italy, France and Spain from the container ships in the Mediterranean was not proven, Crosetto also told us.But cyber-attacks, which he linked to Russia, were now routine - "there are hundreds every day" - and he believed Europe had been too weak in its response."You can't win a war... if you don't fight back," the minister said.Additional reporting from Rome by Davide Ghiglione

schema.headline: Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC

title: Trial of German steakhouse heiress Christina Block that sparked a huge spy scandal
description: It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scanda
body: It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history.Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband.There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel.In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage.Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children.There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year.Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire.Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark.They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others.The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment.Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car.On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands.The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-Württemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg.Christina Block, Andreas Costard and Jonathan G are charged with the abduction of minors, grievous bodily harm and unlawful detention.Block's partner, a former TV sports presenter called Gerhard Delling, and three others are charged with aiding and abetting.All of them deny wrongdoing, except for Jonathan G, who has admitted his involvement. However, he told the court he thought he was taking part in a rescue operation.The trial comes after years of legal battles between Christina Block and her former husband, Stephan Hensel, over who had the right to look after the children.Immediately after their separation, all four children lived with their mother in Hamburg. Hensel, who remarried, later moved to Denmark, where they regularly visited him.In 2021, the two youngest children went to visit their father in Denmark, but then were not brought back to Hamburg as agreed.A court in Hamburg ruled that Christina had custody and that the children should be returned. However, in February 2023, a Danish court ruled that, although the boy and the girl had been brought to Denmark unlawfully, they could not be taken back.In May 2023, Hensel was charged with the abduction of minors, in a case which is still pending.He has accused Christina of being violent with the children, charges she denies. She told the court Hensel wanted to take revenge on her.She also denied knowing anything about plans for the abduction of the children from Denmark. Her defence argues that the Israeli security team had acted on its own initiative.She told the court it was "a catastrophe" and that she had never wanted anything like that.The head of the Israeli security team, David Barkay, who is not on trial but faces future legal proceedings, told the court that Christina Block and Costard had known about the planned repatriation operation.Barkay, who was described by another witness as a former agent with Mossad, the Israeli secret service, said he had not shared all the details because he "didn't trust them."The alleged connection with Germany's former spy chief, August Hanning, relates to accusations of an earlier attempt to abduct the children and bring them back from Denmark in 2022.Prosecutors have said Hanning was responsible for arranging security staff sent to Denmark with Christina Block. His lawyer denies the accusations. Hanning has not been charged over the current Block court case.However, while investigators were searching his home, they came across evidence to suggest Hanning was involved in buying some 2,000 documents from his former chief of staff and then passing on state secrets to foreign powers. Which foreign power and who he is alleged to have given the secrets to is unspecified, but it has prompted widespread speculation.Now 80, Hanning is in custody charged with treasonous espionage. His lawyer says he is being "unjustly persecuted" and that the charges are "unfounded".Meanwhile the trial against Christina Block is currently on hold for two weeks - one of numerous delays and extensions over the course of the past 15 months.The latest delay is because a witness, Stephan Hensel's new wife, failed to appear in court.

schema.headline: Trial of German steakhouse heiress Christina Block that sparked a huge spy scandal

title: The Sabrina Carpenter clip that helped a 22-year-old make £120,000 a year
description: Eknoor Singh says he only needs his mobile phone and a decent internet connection to earn more than £120,000 a year.The 22-year-old Londoner is a prof
body: Eknoor Singh says he only needs his mobile phone and a decent internet connection to earn more than £120,000 a year.The 22-year-old Londoner is a professional "clipper". He is paid by clients to make short, vertical videos for social media, in the hope of them going viral."The more views a clip gets, the more money I make," he says.The way it typically works is that the client - who could be anyone from a clothing brand to a record label, movie studio, podcaster or influencer - has a longer video that the clipper watches first.He or she then makes 30 to 60-second clips of what they consider to be the best bit or bits, and uploads them to Instagram, YouTube, TikTok or other platforms.The idea is that the clippers, who are typically aged from 16 to 25, will have a better understanding of what will connect with that demographic, and get the short videos as many views as possible.For 24-year-old clipper Ethan Weems from Wichita, Kansas, it's a lucrative side hustle to his other video-making work. He says he makes "at least $1,000 a month" from clipping.He does this by making short videos for YouTuber and podcaster Caleb Hammer, who is best known for hosting a show called Financial Audit, which analyses the personal finances of his guests.Weems says clipping helps him make a living from home – giving him more time to spend with his wife and one-year-old son. "I don't want that typical nine-to-five job where I have to go into an office every day," he says.Yet while some clippers can make good money, social media consultant Lia Haberman cautions that there are very few of them. "It mirrors the creator economy more broadly. The vast majority make little to nothing," she says.Meanwhile, streaming industry analyst Devin Nash says it's easy to underestimate the time required to make clipping a success. He warns that successful clippers must "watch hours and hours of content, and they just live in that world".Connecting clippers with their prospective clients are a number of intermediary websites, where available video jobs are listed. These range from pages on general online forums such as Reddit and Discord, to dedicated clipping sites such as Clipping Culture, Vyro, Whop and Kick.The latter websites take a fee from the companies wanting the work done. Clipping Culture lists clients including Capital Records, Universal Music Group and HBO Max.For firms such as these, hiring a teenager or 20-something working from his or her bedroom is far cheaper than paying for traditional adverts on social media, and likely to be more effective in terms of getting eyeballs.That's the experience of Boxabl, a Las Vegas-based firm that makes modular homes. "I think we've done probably a billion views [of clips] so far," says founder Galiano Tiramani, who features in many of the company's videos.In the UK, Jimmy McLoughlin, a former Downing Street adviser and now host of the Jimmy's Jobs of the Future podcast, has also embraced clips."The clips are almost like trailers for the main events," he says. For instance, a recent podcast with Prime Minister Andy Burnham "had close to 50,000 long plays, but in terms of clips, it's done millions".

schema.headline: The Sabrina Carpenter clip that helped a 22-year-old make £120,000 a year

title: Two-week half terms - the school holiday no-one can agree on
description: Samantha Buckland is bracing herself for a tough fortnight. The single mum lives in Reigate, Surrey, and her seven-year-old son goes to a state school
body: Samantha Buckland is bracing herself for a tough fortnight. The single mum lives in Reigate, Surrey, and her seven-year-old son goes to a state school that has just introduced a two-week half term.Buckland has two jobs: teaching medical students at a hospital in Brighton and working at a vintage shop in her home town. The 45-year-old receives universal credit and is worried about the cost of looking after her son while school is closed."What I'm trying to do is find out who I can get childcare from and work around that," she says. "I'd like to work, I need money. It's not cheap to live these days."But money isn't Buckland's only concern. She's also trying to piece together the patchwork of childcare needed to cover the break.There's a local holiday club, but it's only running for one of the two weeks, which Buckland says "parents are up in arms about". She'll also have to work at the hospital some days.As a result, she's considering asking family to help, or even going to stay with a fellow mum so they can take turns with the kids.The number of pupils in England attending academies has grown rapidly in the past decade, according to Department for Education data, external published in June 2026. Indeed, 60.4% of all pupils now attend an academy.As academies spread, the school calendar is becoming increasingly fragmented - creating fresh challenges for parents.Alistair Pringle, 42, lives in Washington in Tyne and Wear with his wife, a teacher, and two children aged 11 and six. His eldest has just started at a secondary academy with a two-week half term, while his youngest goes to a primary academy with a one-week half term."This is the first time we've had to deal with different half terms," Pringle says. His children and wife will be off together for the first week. His eldest then has a second week off, but by then the others will have returned to class.Pringle works full-time in marketing - often in the office - but is fortunate his employer "can accommodate it if I need to work from home"."The thing that concerns me is not so much the childcare, it's the fact that I have to work," he says. "Yes, my eldest would be at home and she'd be looked after, but what's she getting out of that second week?"Parents paid by the hour and those in less flexible jobs, such as those working unsociable or set hours, or in specific locations like hospitals or shops, told BBC News two-week half terms could be particularly challenging.Annual leave is also a big issue. Full-time workers should get at least 28 days' paid annual leave per year, but this is well below the average amount of school holiday.Workers are entitled to take up to 18 weeks' unpaid parental leave for each child up to their 18th birthday. They can't take more than four weeks in a single year, however, and the cost of taking time off makes it an unrealistic option for many.But a two-week break can work well for parents, depending on their circumstances, often allowing families to take a cheaper holiday rather than paying over the odds in peak season. Fay Harding is a fan. The 43-year-old lives in Nottingham with her husband, a teacher at a local authority-run school, and three children at academies. Because her husband and children all go to schools with two-week half terms and are all off at the same time, she says "we don't have to worry about additional childcare costs".Harding's family is planning to spend the first week visiting family in Wales, then she'll work the second week while her husband looks after the children."It also gives us the opportunity to have two weeks away," she says. "We don't have to pay premium prices in the summer."Lucy Walker-Etchells, 40, is a teacher at Dixons Brooklands Academy in south Manchester. Her school has a two-week half term, but for the majority of her teaching career she's had one week."I definitely much prefer two weeks," Walker-Etchells says. "Most teachers would agree because autumn is an intense term. It's really nice to have two weeks to recharge and come back feeling refreshed."Moving a week's holiday from the summer to the autumn half term could benefit pupils too, she believes."Sometimes, vulnerable students really struggle being off for so long over the six-week holiday if they're in difficult circumstances," she says. "That's a long time out of structure, so I don't think it's a bad thing to break up the summer holidays."Unity Schools Partnership runs 40 primary, secondary and special schools across the east of England. The trust introduced a two-week half term in autumn 2023 and asked parents and staff how they felt about the switch the following year.Their consultation found 58% of parents were in favour of the two-week break, with the remainder against. Strikingly, 89% of staff supported it."It's cited as a reason why they would stay with us as an employer, which helps us build quality in schools," says Dominic Norrish, Unity's chief executive.He adds that the number of days lost to staff sickness absence has fallen by 16% since the two-week half term was brought in. "People are getting ill less frequently because they've got longer to recover between half terms," he reflects.Ultimately, getting the best teachers in front of pupils more regularly means "children will receive a better education in the autumn term".

schema.headline: Two-week half terms - the school holiday no-one can agree on

title: Canada 24-21 England: Red Roses' 41-match unbeaten run ends in Toronto
description: Figure caption, Late Canada fightback ends Red Roses' unbeaten streakByElizabeth BotcherbyBBC Sport journalistUpdated 43 minutes agoWXV Global SeriesC
body: Figure caption, Late Canada fightback ends Red Roses' unbeaten streakByElizabeth BotcherbyBBC Sport journalistUpdated 43 minutes agoWXV Global SeriesCanada (5) 24Tries: Bauder, Corrigan, Menin, Seumanutafa Cons: De Goede (2)England (14) 21Tries: Feaunati, Harrison, Bern Cons: Harrison (3)England head coach John Mitchell challenged his Red Roses to "find something more" after their 41-match unbeaten streak - dating back almost four years - ended in dramatic fashion as Shoshanah Seumanutafa's late try handed Canada a thrilling 24-21 victory in Toronto.Canada, who previously snapped England's 39-match winning run with a 26-26 draw in Exeter in September, are the first team to defeat them since November 2022, when they lost to New Zealand in the World Cup final.Playing in front of 18,621 fans, a record for a standalone women's fixture in North America, the result also marks England's first defeat by Canada since 2016 and their first against their hosts on Canadian soil, having won their previous 11 away matches.Canada's Savannah Bauder took advantage of Zoe Harrison's yellow card to open the scoring in the 15th minute, but it was England who took a 14-5 half-time lead, hitting back late in the first half through Maddie Feaunati and Harrison, with Laetitia Royer in the sin-bin for the hosts.Sarah Bern cancelled out a stylish solo try from the hosts' Alysha Corrigan early in the second half to preserve England's nine-point lead before Canada's DaLeaka Menin crashed over for a converted score just after the hour mark to set up a tense finale.Three minutes from time, Canada mounted an attack from halfway after a fumble put Harrison's clearing kick under pressure, and replacement Seumanutafa charged down the left wing to complete the comeback."We're disappointed by the result but there was some very good things in our performance. So we'll stick to our processes," said Mitchell, following his first defeat since being appointed in late 2023. "I guess [the loss] frees us up and allows us to find more. I know this group has got more in them. Sometimes it requires the context that we've just received to dig deeper and find something more."The two sides will renew their rivalry in Ottawa on Friday, 23 October (in the early hours of Saturday on UK time) before England conclude their 2026 WXV Global Series against the USA in New Jersey on Friday, 30 October (21:15 GMT).'We're still world champions, we're still number one'This result has been coming for England, who showcased vulnerability in their three WXV Global Series home matches in September.Against Australia, the world champions trailed at half-time for the first time since 2020 before roaring back with seven second-half tries for a 48-15 win. The following week, Canada held them to a draw in Exeter while a nail-biting 26-19 win over New Zealand at Twickenham was secured with the clock in the red. This time, Canada's defensive resilience in the face of repeated attacks kept the world champions off the scoreboard until the 32nd minute, but England also lacked a clinical touch in their opponents' 22, with multiple opportunities going begging. Notably, Claudia Moloney-MacDonald had an early try chalked off for a knock-on in the grounding.In defence, multiple penalties afforded Canada the freedom to form free-flowing attacks while it was an individual handling error when delivering the ball to fly-half Harrison which gave the hosts field position to score their match-winning try.The result places England in uncharted territory, with several players in the squad never having tasted defeat on the international stage - winger Jess Breach was unbeaten in her previous 59 caps.But for captain Meg Jones, it is no time to panic. England are "still world champions" and her message is simple: "Stick together, look out for each other, and we go again."She added: "We've got to remember, there's a target on our back continuously. Everyone's got that underdog mentality, that underdog fight."We've got to be in a position now where we've got to be the quickest to respond. That's the nature of the game."What an amazing achievement for us as a group. I think they will go down in history as one of the best sporting teams. "We're still world champions, we're still number one, and we'll still keep pushing to be the best we possibly can."Canada avenge World Cup final defeatIn September, Canada captain Sophie de Goede confessed she still has sleepless nights about her side's World Cup final defeat by England in 2025.Even after ending the Red Roses' winning run in Exeter, she was frustrated at being denied the opportunity to go for the win, although reluctantly conceding that head coach Kevin Rouet's call to kick the ball dead was the sensible one.After a historic performance in Toronto, where De Goede's side showcased "the DNA of our team" and "found a way to win", sleep might once again be hard to come by – albeit for far happier reasons.While several Canadian players play their club rugby in England's Premiership Women's Rugby, the national side – ranked third in the world – does not benefit from the same facilities or depth of talent as the Red Roses, even launching a crowdfunding campaign before the last World Cup to cover the cost of their training camps.In the aftermath of their run to the final, the country's government announced a new 775m Canadian dollars (£401m) fund for sport in Canada.Achieving both an attendance record and victory over England in their first home match since August 2025 demonstrates the growing momentum behind women's rugby in the country."It's a little bit more than just the score at the end because we won on so many levels," added scrum-half Justine Pelletier. "Off the field, the crowd, being home. That win at the end on the pitch was just the cherry on [top]."It was good to beat England but I think for a few years now, we knew that we could beat them. It was just a matter of time and a matter of putting every detail together."Line-upsEngland: Kildunne; Breach, Jones, Heard, Moloney-MacDonald; Harrison, L Packer; Botterman, Cokayne, Bern, Talling, Ives Campion, Burton, Matthews, Feaunati.Replacements: Field, Carson, Muir, Short, Kabeya, Hunt, Rowland, Sing.Sin-bin: Harrison (13)Canada: Bauder; Corrigan, Symonds, Perry, Hogan-Rochester; Tessier, Apps; Nelson, Idowu, Menin, de Goede, Royer, Smith, Omokhuale, Gibson.Replacements: Tuttosi, Kassil, Rempel, Forteza, Buisa, Senft, Pelletier, Seumanutafa.Sin-bin: Royer (30)OfficialsReferee: Aurelie Groizeleau (Fra)Assistant referees: Luke Rogan (USA) and Amelia Luciano (USA)TMO: Derek Summers (USA)

schema.headline: Canada 24-21 England: Red Roses' 41-match unbeaten run ends in Toronto

title: Paul Green: Ex-Chelsea WSL chief 'had so many medals under the bed'
description: When Paul Green left Chelsea after 13 years, he had achieved so much success that the majority of his medals were hidden away in a box under the bed.I
body: When Paul Green left Chelsea after 13 years, he had achieved so much success that the majority of his medals were hidden away in a box under the bed.It was only when he had gone that he truly began to appreciate what he had done.The former Chelsea head of women's football formed a formidable partnership with ex-manager Emma Hayes and helped lead the Blues to 19 major trophies.He left suddenly in February amid reports of unrest in Chelsea's hierarchy. Asked about his exit, Green told BBC Sport: "Look, football clubs move on and a lot of people have changed at that club in recent years. "I think ultimately they chose to go in a different direction but I feel very proud of the job that I did there and I left the club in a lot better position than when I first went in there."Under Green's leadership, Chelsea won six successive Women's Super League titles, the last coming under current manager Sonia Bompastor in 2025.They became the most dominant force in the WSL and reached the Women's Champions League final in 2021."It was an incredible time. There was a lot of potential that Emma Hayes sold to me and that came to fruition," said Green. "What the [players] went on to achieve, in my eyes, will never be beaten and it will be difficult for any team to replicate that type of dominance. "It was some of the best times of my life. It's probably not until you're out of it that you actually appreciate what the success was. "I had so many medals that were just chucked under the bed in a box. I've had time to get them framed. Now I've got a new chapter here at Bay FC."Green had seven months out of football before he was appointed as chief football officer of San Francisco club Bay FC in September.He admitted the response to his Chelsea exit had been "overwhelming" and he needed time to adapt, spending time with his family in the meantime."It was people just in the general women's football world who really appreciated the work and success that we had there," said Green."Of course, that touched me and it took me forever to get back to everybody who had reached out because there was that many. "I guess all things have to come to an end at some stage and I've gone in a different direction now."In the early days, having a lack of structure was difficult because I had gone from 13 years of having certain routines. That part was difficult."It is clear that Green is excited by the future at Bay FC.He has taken over a project that is being led by former Football Association (FA) director Kay Cossington and comes under the multi-club ownership of Bay Collective.Green hopes to use his extensive knowledge in the transfer market to recruit some of the world's best players and to build an effective organisation. "They sold me the vision for the club. It became too good an opportunity to turn down," said Green."The potential there of building something really special is what I'm looking forward to. I think it's got some similarities to the early days at Chelsea."Bay FC are moving into new training facilities next year and Green has vowed to act in the transfer window to improve their league position.They are currently third bottom with three matches left in the National Women's Soccer League 2026 season."The team hasn't done as well as everybody would like it to do. We are where we are in the league so we need to try and improve the roster immediately," said Green."With the connections and network that I've built up over 20 years, I'm confident that I can bring in a few players to help the good nucleus of talent we've got."You have to have the infrastructure right off the pitch in terms of staffing and facilities and that's something we are working on."During Green's time at Chelsea, he oversaw the development of several English players including homegrown talents Aggie Beever-Jones and Lexi Potter.Potter made her debut in England's 5-0 win over Greece last week, while Beever-Jones was part of the squad who won Euro 2025.However, there is concern for the future of England's youngsters with gametime for homegrown players reducing in recent years.What does Green suggest the solution is?"Players still need exposure and the way we tried to do it at Chelsea was by having a good loan programme," said Green."You need to find the right partner club to develop the player. But if you haven't got that resource, maybe young players have to go abroad to play."There is the proposal of a 'B team' that a lot of other European leagues have that works very successfully in Germany and Spain. "I do think if they came in at level three of the pyramid that would help because the academy isn't what it used to be. I know that's very controversial."The FA's director of women's football Sue Day said it was an area that needs addressing, while England manager Sarina Wiegman admitted her concern."Not enough of our young players are playing enough football and I think we'd all agree with that," said Day."I don't think you ever want to, even if you could, impose anything regulatory. We all need to work together in this system to make it work. "The FA, the clubs and the league are all on the same side. Clubs are going to create value from investment they are putting into developing players."

schema.headline: Paul Green: Ex-Chelsea WSL chief 'had so many medals under the bed'

title: Vaping: Why people who have never smoked are getting hooked
description: When vaping first took off at Gracey Mungulu's school, she was vocal about the fact she found it as repulsive as smoking."I literally used to tell peo
body: When vaping first took off at Gracey Mungulu's school, she was vocal about the fact she found it as repulsive as smoking."I literally used to tell people like, 'Er, why are you doing that?'" she says.But Gracey says the habit became so common among her classmates that by the age of 16 she too had taken it up, even though the first time left her coughing rather than inhaling."The more you see it, the more you start trying it a bit more," Gracey says, "and then eventually I just got used to it and I was just doing it all the time."Now 21, she buys a refillable vape every day, using it whenever her hands aren't busy with her work as a hairdresser and in a school.Gracey is among the more than one million people in the UK who say they have never smoked but now vape, according to recent Office for National Statistics (ONS) survey data – and that number has risen year-on-year.When vaping first came to the market it was seen as a way to help smokers quit cigarettes.Vaping nicotine, a highly addictive substance, is less harmful than cigarettes, but the long-term effects are not yet clear, according to the NHS.So why are people like Gracey, who have never smoked a cigarette, taking it up?The Londoner believes vaping helps when she's feeling socially anxious."It's the hand action," she says, "just having something in your hand, just having something in your mouth."Like cigarettes Gracey's vape contains nicotine, a highly addictive substance that triggers withdrawal symptoms like irritability and anxiety when it leaves your system.Vaping has become a "mindless action," she says. When she answers the call to talk to BBC News for this article, Gracey says that without thinking about it, she had been lying in bed, with her vape in one hand, and her other hand scrolling Instagram.The habitual aspect of regular vaping is something GP Dr Helen Wall hears a lot from her patients."It's that kind of psychological dependence on something else to almost regulate their emotions," she says.Like Gracey, Malin Andersson, who vaped until recently, says her habit went hand in hand with doomscrolling. She had also tried cigarettes but never considered herself a smoker.At 33, she falls in the age range most likely to vape. The ONS report suggests nearly one in six people aged 25-34 in the UK may use e-cigarettes daily or occasionally.The domestic abuse campaigner and former Love Island contestant started vaping when she was going through a stressful break-up and looking for comfort. She believes it was the physical action that got her hooked."It's a dopamine hit," Malin says. "It's literally an adult's version of a dummy."She says it was dulling her senses and leaving her demotivated.Malin became so frustrated with how reliant she had become on her banana ice-flavoured vape that she quit in May this year."It was annoying me so much that it was always in my hand that I'd end up throwing it across the room," she says. Alex, from Manchester, also gradually formed a vaping habit, which started after she occasionally vaped on nights out and then began to take the vapes home.The 26-year-old, who didn't want to give her last name, says the habit would become such a constant part of her life that she would work while "lying in my bed with my laptop in front of me and then my vape on my chest".Prof Sarah Jackson, from the University College London Alcohol and Tobacco Research Group, points out that while "alarm bells" may ring at the recent ONS figures, it could be the case that some of the people in this group would have started smoking if they hadn't started vaping."In which case, vaping has diverted them away from a more harmful behaviour, which is good news," she says. "On the other hand, there will be people that are being exposed to more risk than they would have otherwise."She points to a 2024 study from UCL researchers that found nicotine use had risen among young adults in England, although cigarette smoking had declined. "We can infer from that that some of the people who are vaping wouldn't have smoked otherwise," Jackson says.The ONS report says about 5.4 million people aged 16 and over vape in Britain, while the number of smokers of all ages continues to steadily fall. Some 4.9 million adults in the UK  smoke.The UK is aiming to cut smoking rates and reduce the appeal of vaping among children and young people.The marketing of vapes - which has featured bright colours and sweet flavours - is being looked at, with a recent government consultation on new measures expected to give a response in due course.Within the 1.1 million vapers who never smoked, "there probably is a group who would not be vaping [without] the marketing of vaping which is very prominent", says Hazel Cheeseman from charity Action on Smoking and Health.The NHS warns non-smokers and those aged 17 and under to never vape, while it's illegal for anyone under 18 to buy vapes. Disposable vapes - seen as a key driver in the rise of youth vaping – were banned last year.Wall says the heavy marketing of vapes in recent years has helped to fuel a "misconception" that they are "safe and not addictive".Gracey thinks vapes should be sold in the same standardised plain packaging as cigarettes because it "looks scary"."With vapes, they have all these flavours, all these pretty colours - it's just making us more attracted to it".While she says vaping is seen as far more socially acceptable among her generation than smoking, she finds her habit problematic and has considered quitting to save the £35 a week it costs her.But just like smoking, giving up vaping can be a struggle. And for Alex, vaping led her in the opposite direction.She says she managed to quit vaping while travelling for several months, but with no access to vapes she began smoking cigarettes for the first time instead.Cigarettes are not considered a healthy or helpful way to stop vaping by experts. The NHS strongly advises people to stop smoking, and it remains the leading cause of preventable illness and premature death in the UK.To quit vaping the NHS suggests gradually reducing the strength of the vape's nicotine, increasing the time between vaping sessions, or switching to a suitable nicotine replacement therapy product. But professional support to stop vaping is patchy, with a recent survey, external finding fewer than half (45%) of healthcare providers in England offered vaping cessation support. There is a mixed picture of support to quit across the rest of the UK. While it is good fewer people are smoking, Wall says that for people like Gracey who go straight to vapes a bit of the messaging has been missed.  "Vaping was only intended [by the NHS] to be a replacement for cigarettes."

schema.headline: Vaping: Why people who have never smoked are getting hooked

title: Man City charges: Do Premier League club have grounds for their appeal?
description: Manchester City face "substantial hurdles" if they are to have any chance of winning their appeal after being found guilty of breaking the Premier Lea
body: Manchester City face "substantial hurdles" if they are to have any chance of winning their appeal after being found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules, a leading lawyer has told BBC Sport.City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, and creating "sham contracts" to inflate sponsorship deals by £830m.The club have said they are "innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League" and they have "irrefutable evidence" the ruling "contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe".In their appeal, City will argue the payments were made by the United Arab Emirates government as a shareholder of the sponsors, while there are inconsistencies in the Commission's judgement. Therefore, City say the sponsorship amounts were legitimate and not topped up by the owners.James Severn, Member of the London Solicitor Litigation Association (LSLA) and Partner at Penningtons Manches Cooper, told BBC Sport the appeal is "not simply an opportunity to invite a new panel" to get the verdict overturned."City will need to identify a material error of law, principle or fact, or serious procedural unfairness, which materially affected the Commission's decision," Severn said. "The Appeal Board nevertheless has broad powers to allow or dismiss the appeal, vary the decision or make any other order it considers appropriate."Etihad Airways, one of City's principle sponsors at the centre of the case, had previously stated that the Abu Dhabi government had not paid for its sponsorship of Manchester City.That came in court documents as part of a US investigation in New York in 2015.City will argue this does not have the full context of the situation and is not proof they have been inconsistent with evidence.The club are adamant government documents fully support their case - but, Severn said, if these were already available to the Commission they may not be much use in an appeal."The bank statements, government records and contemporaneous payment documents could be powerful evidence if they establish a clear audit trail showing the disputed funds came from the Abu Dhabi government rather than the owners," Severn added. "However, if that evidence was already before the Commission, which nevertheless concluded that the arrangements were a sham, City will face an uphill struggle to demonstrate the finding was materially wrong."Shortly before City's appeal was confirmed, Etihad Airways issued a statement saying it had never been "given the opportunity by the Premier League to be represented, to provide relevant information, or to ensure the accuracy and fairness of information relied upon".Severn said Etihad Airways' complaint "does not, of itself, establish procedural unfairness"."Etihad was not the respondent and is unlikely to have had an independent right to participate in the proceedings," Severn said. "It is likely to have been open to either party to obtain and present such evidence to the Commission. "If the Appeal Board is prepared to consider new evidence from Etihad, it is likely to carry greater weight if supported by contemporaneous documents."A key part of City's defence will be that the Independent Commission relied too heavily on the emails obtained through the Football Leaks files."If City can demonstrate the Commission fundamentally misunderstood the emails, failed to consider their proper context or reached conclusions inconsistent with other contemporaneous documents, that could amount to a material factual error," Severn added. "City's difficulty is that the Commission heard extensive witness and documentary evidence but nevertheless made serious findings of sham arrangements and disguised owner funding."Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport the commission found "the documents were retrofitted to fit the crime". "The Commission must have concluded that the evidence and the credibility of the witnesses put up by Manchester City were poor," Maguire said."However, from a legal point of view, this is an area they could attack if Manchester City's team can prove that the commission itself was a flawed construct in the sense that the members were Premier League picks rather than Manchester City's, and therefore the deck was stacked against the club to begin with. "But that seems remote." Severn added that the retired senior judges and leading barristers, who sat on the Commission, have "spent their careers interpreting complicated facts, dealing with witnesses and applying relevant weight to evidence".While adding that it would be "impossible to assess reliably" the chances of City winning their appeal, Severn added that "doing so will not be easy". But Maguire believes that while it will be difficult for City to be successful, "there is a route".City have brought in Mark Howard KC to advise the club in their appeal, while Etihad Airways has enlisted the services of respected law firm Quinn Emanuel.Maguire said: "Given the lawyers that have been recruited by Manchester City, they may go down what's been described to me as a mess and noise approach."That means trying to discredit everything to do with the process of the Commission rather than necessarily the evidence that was presented. "I've seen the documents that Abu Dhabi presented to the New York case. I'm not a lawyer, but from an accounting point of view, they can be seen in more than one way."Even though Premier League regulations state an appeal must be heard within 12 weeks, or by Christmas Eve, Severn added that "given the scale and complexity of the proceedings, a final outcome may not be known for some time".

schema.headline: Man City charges: Do Premier League club have grounds for their appeal?

title: Social media algorithms: What if you could turn them off?
description: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switchFigure caption, Watch: Many social platforms already have following-only feed
body: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switchFigure caption, Watch: Many social platforms already have following-only feeds - here's how they workByTiffanie TurnbullSydneyWarning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorderVarsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day."I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC."I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.Image source, Tiffanie Turnbull / BBCImage caption, Varsha Yajman says social media aggravated her eating disorderIt is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommender content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier.But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.The choiceFlynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order."You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC."I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.Image source, Daniel Fermer / ABC NewsImage caption, Flynn Martin says he's still finding a healthy balance with social mediaNowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction, external; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health, external, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline.Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line."The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.Image source, Cordelia Hsu/ReutersImage caption, Consent education campaigner Chanel Contos lobbied the government for change after founding the Teach Us Consent website in 2021While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change."Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off."This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said."If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them."Image source, Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesImage caption, Communications Minister Anika Wells (left podium) and Australian PM Anthony Albanese (right podium) announcing the upcoming Digital Duty of Care bill The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m)."The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC.The challengesThere's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation.In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive – although a US jury recently ruled otherwise."I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' – like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' – and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney.Image source, Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Instagram chief Adam Mosseri argues recommender algorithms are essential to user enjoymentRight-wing parties in Australia – and the Trump administration – have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship.But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake – they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week.The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children.However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Australian regulators are investigating potential breaches of the social media banThe EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale.Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that."Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation, external.On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return.The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act.Image source, Benjamin Fanjoy/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Meta lost an appeal against the Dutch court's ruling in March, meaning users in the Netherlands retain choice over their home feedsThe rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app.Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global."We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing."Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them.Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment."Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms – though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off.Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice."On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good."If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Social media algorithms: What if you could turn them off?
